question: How does Java pass object arguments to methods during invocation?

options.text: Java passes all arguments strictly by value; for objects, the reference address itself is copied by value.
Java uses pass-by-reference only if the method parameter is declared with double equals syntax.
Java creates a deep clone of the object and passes the cloned copy by value.
Java passes primitive types by value, but passes all object types by true reference.

explanation: Java is strictly pass-by-value. When an object is passed, the value of the reference variable (the memory pointer) is copied into the method parameter.

question: What does the `==` operator compare when evaluated between two object reference variables in Java?

options.text: It checks whether all fields of both objects contain identical data values.
It passes both objects by reference to the JVM runtime comparison routine.
It automatically calls .equals() on the first operand to verify logical equivalence.
It compares reference identity, checking whether both variables point to the exact same memory address.

explanation: The == operator on reference types compares memory addresses. It returns true if and only if both operands point to the exact same object in the heap.
